# Question

**Does eating organic food improve your health?** In the IVL/Coop Sweden within-family pilot (Magnér et al. 2015), one family switched from a conventional to an organic diet for two weeks; urinary pesticide concentrations were measured before, during and after. Lock⁵ ships the raw data as *OrganicEffect* (160 paired measurements).

## Data source

REAL Lock5 dataset (`OrganicEffect`) — exact, verbatim. n = 5 family members × 8 pesticides, paired conventional vs organic measurements. Endpoint is *exposure*, not a clinical health outcome; single family, diet order not randomized.

# Exploratory analysis

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Urinary pesticide concentration, conventional vs organic diet (paired)"
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 4))
ax.boxplot([df["NonOrganic"], df["Organic"]], tick_labels=["Conventional", "Organic"])
ax.set_ylabel("Urinary pesticide (µg/g creatinine)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

# Methods & results

Paired t-test, Wilcoxon signed-rank (non-parametric), sign-flip randomization (100k), bootstrap CI of the mean difference, Cohen's d and percent reduction.

| Method | Result |
|---|---|
| Mean concentration | 38.76 → 2.83 µg/g creatinine (**−92.7%**) |
| Mean diff | +35.93 (bootstrap CI excludes 0), d = 0.37 |
| Paired t | t(159) = 4.71, **p = 5.3e-6** |
| Wilcoxon signed-rank | p = 3.7e-22 |
| Sign-flip randomization (100k) | p < 1e-5 |

# Decision

**Switching to an organic diet dramatically cut pesticide exposure within days** — the cleanest experimental evidence in this whole question set. But the endpoint is exposure rather than a health outcome, and with a single family and non-randomized diet order, generalization is limited.
